chapter: Sanger, Ben Black and carnival balls
title: The Strand, St. Charles, the Sanger and Ben Black, Jules Stein, the Edgewater
summary: One long answer covers the Strand pit, a St. Charles contract, the Sanger side-man job under Ben Black, MCA's Jules Stein and a convention.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: Alright, what about The Strand? I'll bring back an incident. The Strand...

The Strand was a long picture theater. And it had... Most of the time it had Don Filippini as the director. He could get more out of a waltz and most of them could get out of a symphony. Then afterwards it had Castro Carraza who went over to the singer. But he couldn't play Stardust unless he got the record and found out what the tempo was. He didn't know A from a bull's foot but he could stand up there and direct the orchestra. He was stiff as a post. Mr. Barr used to tell him, Castro get down off that sump box. Get down amongst the people. He would never unbend. And the reason why I was in the singer orchestra was because I had a contract for two years at the St. Charles and they had to close up. They didn't have any air conditioning. So Mr. Garinger who was the general manager and a personal friend of mine, he happened to be in Biloxi on vacation. And he says, Johnny that's a nice band you have there. I said, coming from you Mr. Garinger, I said it's quite a compliment. I said that's the band you ought to have in the pit at the St. Charles. That was dramatic stock. Seven nights and two matinees. Just like five days to play golf and go hunting. And played out the dance books. He says come see me when you come to town. So we closed over there Labor Day. I had come see Mr. Garinger. I got a week off. So I said we might as well cash in on this week off but let's get this contract. He said well I want you for two years. He wanted me. I said you can make it ten. Is that kind of a job? I could get the carbs you know. I used to have to hustle. Easiest job in the world. Played a couple. And after they got the scenery set and the weeks that we only used one set I might not finish a tune before the second act would go on. So it was so easy. And still we couldn't take the job properly because one night we didn't play the people out. Half of the guys were playing pool and the other was the bowling alley. And I don't have any band. I can't find any musicians. Well I let it go but I impressed all of them in the future that that was his job you know. But they didn't need to. So that's the kind of job we had. Now I went into this sign of why. Mr. Garinger said Johnny you're one of the family. I said well you put that in writing. He said well we don't know how long we're going to exist but you are one of the family. You'll always have a job. Being a married man I said well that sounds alright. This job and some others will go together you know. So he said we want you to go into the Sanger. You won't have any responsibility. You're just side man. You're in the band. And we give you $135 a week. Well that was pretty fair money in those days. More than I did. I said $135 a week. He said yeah. I said and the extras. Because we had extras. We got $16 a week extras to play the floor show. Play the stage show. And overtime. So some weeks we had some beauts. I remember one week I took 16 encores on Mason Street Blues. How anybody could stomach 16 choruses by me I don't know it. But every time I stopped the house would come down. Ben Black would sing. And Ben Black he was the master's son. I'd be playing Just the Memory. And he'd be saying to the audience isn't that beautiful. Listen to that boy. I'd play Just the Memory you know. I'd play Day is Done. Copy. Copy. And he'd be staring up there with his bat horns. Idolizing old Johnny you know. You can't mess with an MC. And he says I want to tell you fellas something. I'm easy. I don't know at all. I'm only a banjo player. But he had good jobs. He tried to get me to go to Barron Longs and join him in San Francisco. Long before he ever saw my face. He asked my brother and I to join him. He says every man in this band has a car. That meant that they were making money. Because there wasn't so many automobiles in those days I'm telling him. But we didn't want to go to Francisco. So I picked the job. And it was easy. I didn't have much to worry about except that I was featured every week. And who can't play I can't give anything but love on a trumpet for God's sake. And then every MC if you'll notice what they write on there, I was the one that said let's play this, let's play that. Because when Ray Teal came in there, he was my golfing competitor. When he was here. Well they all rocked. I played with everyone. Clyde Lucas, Rory Ballet and all the rest of them. They knew I had a call. I don't know. They liked me. I played trumpet. They knew me. I was one of them. And I could show them where the golf links were. We used to burlesque a lot. You know what I mean. Have a lot of fun. Clyde Lucas used to take his whole family with him when he'd go out. His brother and his father and all walk around. He'd meet a lot of nice people. I met Clyde afterwards at the convention with Jules Stein. Now you know who Jules Stein is. He's the head of MCA. Yeah. I know Mr. Stein very well. I said Mr. Stein what do you do to be a big band? I said I'm pretty big in my own town. He says I know that. Nothing. He said you bring your trumpet. I'll get you all the musicians and all the arrangers you want. Just bring your trumpet. You come. Now that's a nice offer huh. And with Jules Stein. So we're having lunch together in the hotel. I like the Blue Room. And there's one of those fiddle tenor bands up there. I said look at this. Look at that. The tenors are doing. Four tenors. Clyde Lucas says. Don't you think a week of this would push you to crazy house. Listen to that music. And that's one of Jules Stein's bands. Jules said listen Clyde. I make more money off of these kind of bands than I do off of your band. And I don't know if you're a band. I don't know if you're a band. I don't know if you're a band. I don't know if you're a band. They don't want to play in harmony. Yeah. And all those votes are not in the same position. You know that. Can they get up and make a speech about it? Mm-hm. Can he get up and make a speech about it? People will have the bad use of saying, I used to try to tell him not to say it, the public is stupid. The public is our living. The man that you make the most fun of, he got more money in his pocket than anybody in place. He pay every time you're playing on the court. It always developed that way. Not that we look for tips, but we never refused them. Only came in handy for the spaghetti and meatballs. We used to get off at 2 o'clock in the morning at the Edgewater, we'd stop at Fairchild and they'd open the kitchen for us. Because we'd stop there all the time. The guy didn't mind warming up, some leftover spaghetti, it tasted good. We were hungry, starving. But most of the time at the Edgewater, we were well fed. We had a drag with the cook, and I'd tell him we don't have much time. He'd give me a big piece of French bread, fresh, and put a filet mignon in there. I'll tell you what, the butter dripping over it, pickles, I'll tell you that was worse, better than that bag with those people who paid. I'll play the cook for Coca-Cola over there, I'll tell you about that, but the $900? They had over 900 people. And the man wanted the salad fresh. They never served 900 in their life in the Edgewater. How are they going to serve 900 salads? Where are they going to put them in the first place? They don't have the iceboxes. So by the time the people came in, it was wilted. And you know what I had to do? Just played them in. I played every college year that was ever written so I wouldn't miss anybody because you get drunk and punch you in the nose. You don't play at college. The guy come up to the market and said, play Bradley. And I made the mistake. I said, where is Bradley? Ooh, whoop! Where is Bradley? And one of the guys in the band said, that's the basketball team was caught cheating or something. Remember that Miss Cannon? And that was, I want to lick the band. I said, you don't listen. I said, we're kidding you. I said, whistle it to us. He whistled us, Bradley. We played a couple of bars. Because we could fake anything, some of us. And my piano player was a good figure too. He said, you knew Bradley, you didn't want to play.
